seo.title: Karmic tail 21 7 22 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 7 22 compatibility: The World, The Chariot and The Fool in a couple's tail, read through Waite, Wen and Jules Verne's race round the world.

title: The 21-7-22 karmic tail in compatibility: the whole world, the road and a day off the timetable
short: The 21-7-22 karmic tail in compatibility turns the order of the Major Arcana upside down: the couple's task opens with The World, the last card of the deck, and closes with The Fool, the card of beginnings. It belongs to two people who find a shared world before they take a shared step. They agree quickly on the big picture and travel the road in motion and to a plan, and what they have to learn is what others start with: to take the serious step freely, out of trust, and to leave room for the unforeseen.

sections.h2: How to read the 21-7-22 tail in a couple's chart
paragraphs: On the site these three numbers sit in the sphere “The couple's karmic tail” under the captions “Entry to the task” (M), “Middle of the task” (N) and “Main task” (D). Each number is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. The main point is D: it shows what the couple has to learn and is read above all through what does not work.

M is the shared wish with which the two enter the task. The same point appears in the sphere “Relationship and common language” under the caption “Common language”, and the wish in it easily turns into resistance: what the couple wants together starts to hold it in place. N is how the couple lives the road from the wish to the task. This is our site's reading: Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own and calls it an addition to the main task.

In the deck the Major Arcana run from The Fool to The World. For Waite The Fool is zero, the card without a number, and The World is fullness and completion. In the destiny matrix The Fool carries the number 22, right after The World. The 21-7-22 tail walks this road backwards: the couple starts from the result, from a whole world, and its main work lies in the first step.
The tail does not say whether the couple will marry or part, and it sets no dates. It describes the shape of the task: where the two of them find things easy and where they skid.

sections.h2: A novel about a couple, read as a novel about travel
paragraphs: Verne's novel came out in 1872; quotations below follow George Makepeace Towle's English translation of 1873 unless marked otherwise. People remember it as a race with steamers and an elephant. But read next to this tail, another book shows through: two people travel together for eighty days without knowing what they are to each other, and everything is decided by a day that was not on the timetable.

Phileas Fogg lives at No. 7, Saville Row as if the world had already been gone round. He breakfasts and dines at the club at the same hours, at the same table. He has dismissed his last servant for bringing “shaving-water at eighty-four degrees Fahrenheit instead of eighty-six”. His only pastimes are the papers and whist, a game that for him is “a contest, a struggle with a difficulty, yet a motionless, unwearying struggle”. And yet nobody at the club knows the map of the globe better: “He must have travelled everywhere, at least in the spirit.” One more line from the first chapter will be needed at the end: Fogg was not known to have “either relatives or near friends”.

The wager is born at the card table. “The world is big enough,” says a partner. “It was once,” Fogg replies in a low tone. A newspaper has already worked out the route: eighty days. What about storms, wrecks, torn-up rails? “All included.” And delays? “The unforeseen does not exist.” Fogg stakes twenty thousand pounds that he will walk into the club on Saturday, 21 December, at a quarter before nine in the evening — in 1,920 hours. The papers would call the scheme madness.

In India he is joined by Aouda, a young widow he saves from being burned on her husband's funeral pyre. Beside him all the way is Passepartout, his new servant: a former itinerant singer, circus rider and rope dancer who took service with “the most exact and settled gentleman in the United Kingdom” in order “to taste the sweets of domestic life” — and set off round the world that same evening.

The three cards of the tail stand in the novel in order. The World is the wager on the whole globe, gone round in the head beforehand. The Chariot is eighty days of steamers, trains, sledges and connections. The Fool is the evening when all is lost, and the question Aouda asks.

sections.h2: The World at the entry: “All included”
paragraphs: In Waite's divinatory list The World upright means “Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”, and reversed “Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence”. In the novel's first chapters the two lists stand side by side. Fogg in London is The World reversed: the same hours, the same table, water at exactly eighty-six degrees. The wager is The World upright: a route, a voyage, a promised reward. This is how the “Entry to the task” works: the wish for a whole world and the resistance to it live in one point.
Even “emigration” from the list is in the book. In Hong Kong it turns out that the relative Aouda was travelling to has gone to live in Europe, and her road becomes a shared road with Fogg.

Wen calls The World “the card of synthesis” and recalls the Gaia hypothesis: the world as a living, evolving organism. Fogg's world is a table from a newspaper: London to Suez, seven days; Suez to Bombay, thirteen; total, eighty. The difference between a living world and a timetable of the world is the first thing worth seeing for a couple with this tail.

In life the entry looks like this. Two people meet, and within a month they share a map. They think alike about money and freedom, they want to live by the sea or in another country, they have agreed that each stays themselves and the chores are split in half. They talk until three in the morning about how it will all be. Friends call them the perfect couple, and that is no exaggeration: the two really do speak one language, and that language is the language of the big picture.

The resistance grows out of the same picture. A world drawn together is no longer redrawn. When one of them changes — a new job, a new circle, a new wish — the other hears it as a betrayal of the shared plan and starts correcting: “but we agreed”. The same holiday route every year, the same arguments to the same script, and the most dangerous sentence of all: “we already know everything about ourselves”. Fogg would put it more briefly: “All included.”

sections.h2: The Chariot in the middle: “not travelling, but only describing a circumference”
paragraphs: The middle of the task shows how the couple travels the road, and with this tail it travels on The Chariot. The novel has a sentence that describes this card better than any handbook. On a train in India General Cromarty would gladly tell his fellow passenger about the country, but Fogg asks nothing: **“Phileas Fogg, who was not travelling, but only describing a circumference,** took no pains to inquire into these subjects; he was a solid body, traversing an orbit around the terrestrial globe, according to the laws of rational mechanics.” The general studies him and wonders “whether a human heart really beat beneath this cold exterior”.

Mechanics reaches this card from two sides. Wen, explaining The Chariot, writes that “Key 7 might be likened to Newton's second law of motion: force is mass times acceleration”, and The Chariot is the force that is enough to accelerate the mass of the problem. Waite calls the charioteer “above all things triumph in the mind”. Almost a century and a half before Wen, Verne described his hero in the words of the same physics: a body, an orbit, the laws of mechanics.

But Waite's divinatory list for The Chariot does not open with victory; it opens with “Succour, providence”. And when Fogg's machine leaves the schedule of its own accord, it is to help: in India he saves Aouda, on the American prairie he goes to rescue Passepartout, taken by a war party. In the jungle the guide tells them of the widow who is to be burned at dawn. “Suppose we save this woman.” — “I have yet twelve hours to spare; I can devote them to that.” The general is astonished: “Why, you are a man of heart!” “Sometimes,” replied Phileas Fogg, quietly; “when I have the time.” Those words hold the whole danger of the tail's middle: the heart is there, but it switches on by the timetable.

From then on Aouda travels with him, and her position is never named. “What ought I to do, Mr. Fogg?” — “It is very simple… Go on to Europe… You do not intrude, nor do you in the least embarrass my project. Passepartout!… Go to the ‘Carnatic,’ and engage three cabins.” On board he visits her at fixed hours, listens, makes sure she wants for nothing, but “with the precision of an automaton, the movements of which had been arranged for this purpose. Aouda did not quite know what to make of him.”

Near the end The Chariot shows what speed costs. In the middle of the Atlantic the steamer Henrietta runs short of coal. Fogg buys the ship and has her wood burned in the furnaces: “the poop, cabins, bunks, and the spare deck were sacrificed.” The next day the masts go. The ship burns its own cabins so as not to lose speed.

A couple with this tail recognises itself in the best chapters of the race. They are a team: they move house, renovate, start a business together, pull each other out of trouble and stand up for each other in front of strangers. Each goes their own way, but side by side, and it is exciting to travel together.

And it recognises itself in the worst. Conversation shrinks to logistics: who is meeting whom, where the connection is, whether the bill is paid. Talking about “us” can happen when there is time — after the move, after the project, after the holiday. There is a quiet struggle for the reins: who drives. Tiredness comes out as irritation over nothing. One expects the other to put a goal aside for the sake of the shared route. And the cabins go into the furnace — sleep, weekends, a home where one can simply be. Among the tasks of The Chariot in a couple Lisovskaya names this one too: learning to restore strength with care instead of taking it from those close by.

sections.h2: The Fool as the main task: what are we to each other?
paragraphs: In Waite The Fool has two faces, and Waite himself keeps them apart. In the symbolic account The Fool is “the spirit in search of experience”, “a prince of the other world on his travels through this one”. In the divinatory list he is “Folly, mania, extravagance, intoxication, delirium, frenzy, bewrayment”, and reversed “Negligence, absence, distribution, carelessness, apathy, nullity, vanity”.

In the novel The Fool appears in both forms. In Verne's French the papers call Fogg a maniaque and a fou, a maniac and a madman (our translation; Towle has “lunatic”) — words from the same roots as “mania” and “folly” at the head of Waite's list. The journey swallows nearly nineteen thousand pounds: an elephant for two thousand, a steamer bought for firewood. And at the pyre in India Fogg has to be held back by force, because he, “in an instant of mad generosity, was about to rush upon the pyre”. The folly of the wager and the generous folly are two different Fools, and the couple's task is to tell one from the other.

The main task of the tail is read through what does not work, and with The Fool that is above all uncertainty. What is Aouda during those eighty days? A rescued woman, a fellow traveller, a guest, a ward? Three cabins. Fogg looks after her flawlessly and says not one word about what is between them. Wen writes of The Fool reversed: “If in a relationship, it is a spontaneous one.” And of The World reversed, that such a person “thrives in ambiguity”, is at home in it like a fish in water. On the downside the two cards of the tail meet on one thing: it suits both partners not to name anything.

A couple with this tail can live for years in such a “for now”. Together, but without a name: not husband and wife, not “just seeing each other”, but “we have our own kind of relationship”. Everything begins easily and beautifully, and as soon as it comes to a serious step — moving in, getting married, taking out a joint loan, moving abroad together — one of them suddenly has an urgent trip, a new project, a “let's do it later”. The freedom both were proud of turns into two flatmates with a shared calendar. There is a flip side as well: the one who dislikes rules starts to be jealous and to check up, and at the first difficulty walks out with a reproach — “you were the one who said we didn't need a piece of paper”.

The upside of The Fool in a couple is trust, and freedom grows out of it. The two do not check up on each other, each is self-sufficient and enters the union consciously, they can laugh and start from zero. The task is not to crush The Fool inside and become a Fogg with a daily routine. The task is to make the leap.

In the novel Aouda makes it, at the worst moment possible. Fogg is sure he came back to London five minutes too late: the wager is lost, the fortune gone. In the evening he comes to apologise for bringing her to England, where he can no longer provide for her. “But what will become of you, Mr. Fogg?” — “As for me, madam, I have need of nothing.” “Your friends—” — “I have no friends, madam.” “Your relatives—” — “I have no longer any relatives.” And then she rises: **“Mr. Fogg, do you wish at once a kinswoman and friend? Will you have me for your wife?”**

Her question answers the first chapter, where Fogg was not known to have “either relatives or near friends”. For eighty days the status had no name — and now it is named in one sentence. Fogg shuts his eyes, opens them and says: “I love you!… I am entirely yours!” The Fool has stepped off the edge, and the edge here is real: ruin.

sections.h2: The day that was not on the timetable
paragraphs: Passepartout runs to the Reverend Samuel Wilson to arrange the wedding for tomorrow, Monday, and soon comes back without his hat, knocking passers-by over. “Marriage—impossible… Impossible—for to-morrow.” — “Why so?” — “Because to-morrow—is Sunday!” — “Monday,” replied Mr. Fogg. — “No—to-day is Saturday… You have made a mistake of one day!”

Fogg has lived the whole day as 22 December, and it was the 21st. There are ten minutes left before the wager closes. A cab, a hundred pounds promised to the driver, two dogs run over, five carriages overturned — and he walks into the club saloon as the clock shows a quarter before nine.

Verne gives the solution with figures. Travelling east, towards the sun, Fogg shortened his day by four minutes for every degree of longitude; three hundred and sixty degrees at four minutes each make exactly one day. He saw the sun pass the meridian eighty times, his partners in London seventy-nine.

The secret was written in the book long before the ending. Back in India General Cromarty explained to Passepartout that, going eastward, “the days were shorter by four minutes for each degree gone over”. Passepartout “obstinately refused to alter his watch”; already in Suez he had told the detective: “So much the worse for the sun, monsieur. The sun will be wrong, then!” And in the very first chapter, hiring him, Fogg notes that the new servant's watch is exactly four minutes slow: “No matter; it's enough to mention the error.” The novel opens with four minutes and closes with the same four minutes multiplied by 360.

Now the main thing. Fogg names the cause of his victory himself. In the evening he tells Aouda: **“If you had not suggested our marriage, my servant would not have gone to the Reverend Samuel Wilson's, I should not have been apprised of my error, and—”** The error in the calendar was uncovered not by calculation and not by speed, but by the decision to marry. The serious step gave back the whole world.

That is the hidden plot of the 21-7-22 tail. The couple's main task, The Fool, is not the price of the road and not an obstacle on it, but the key to the entry. While the two race by the timetable, they feel they are late and have lost everything. Clarity about what they are to each other gives them back a day that was not on the calendar: time that, it turns out, they had in hand.

The morning after the wedding Passepartout bursts in with a discovery: the world could have been gone round in seventy-eight days. “No doubt,” returned Mr. Fogg, “by not crossing India. But if I had not crossed India, I should not have saved Aouda; she would not have been my wife, and—” The shortest route is The Chariot's route. The detour on which the meeting happened is the couple's route.

This ending has a forerunner. In 1841 Edgar Allan Poe published a story he later called “Three Sundays in a Week”. An old uncle promises Kate to the hero “when three Sundays come together in a week” — that is, never. The condition is met by two sea captains who have sailed round the globe in opposite directions: for one Sunday was yesterday, for the other it will be tomorrow. The bride is the first to see the answer, and a captain sums it up: “there can be no philosophical reason assigned why the idea of one of us should have preference over that of the other.” Whether Verne knew the story has not been established. But in both, an extra day settles a question of marriage, each side keeps its own time, and both are right.

Three coincidences are worth recording precisely as coincidences, with no conclusions drawn. The novel's decisive mix-up is between 21 and 22 December, and the couple's tail ends with the same numbers: The World and The Fool. The Paris daily Le Temps ran the novel from 6 November to 22 December 1872, so the last instalment appeared the day after Fogg's deadline. And Wen, timing The Chariot by the sign of Cancer, gives the dates “June 21–July 22”. The numbers of the tail do not steer the plots of books, but coincidences like these are easy to remember.

sections.h2: What the numbers of the 21-7-22 tail show
paragraphs: The 21-7-22 tail occurs in about one couple in 84 (1.19%) and ranks 30th among the 97 couple tails. It cannot be a personal tail: in a personal chart the entry M is the main task D plus the centre, and with D = 22 an entry of 21 is impossible with any centre. This tail exists only between two people.
It is built from four combinations of the partners' personal tails:

This table holds three clues. The first: none of the tail's three cards appears in either partner's personal tail — no World, no Chariot, no Fool. The tail is born only in the sum; on their own, neither partner has it.

The second: in all four combinations the middle is 25, reduced to 7. Two personal paths added together do not fit into the deck and fold into The Chariot. This couple's Chariot belongs to no one: it is the speed of two, not the habit of one.

The third: the entry is always an exact sum of the two personal entries, 15 + 6 or 12 + 9. Were the couple a single person with the main task 22 and The Star at the centre, the personal formula would give the entry 22 + 17 = 39 → 12, The Hanged Man. The couple has 21 at the entry — the same digits in reverse. The Hanged Man is the card of suspended waiting; this couple enters its task not through waiting but straight through a whole world, because the entry is put together by two.

And one more piece of arithmetic. In three combinations out of four (77% of couples) one partner enters their personal tail through The Devil (15) and the other through The Lovers (6), and the shared World at the entry is their sum. The same two cards become the couple's values: The Lovers in 71.1%, The Devil in 28.9%. The points and the calculation are different here, so this is arithmetic only; our reading is that this couple's world is made of choice and attachment.

sections.h2: The Star at the centre and the couple's values
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the atmosphere between the two, what is not on show. In 96.7% of couples with this tail it holds The Star, in 3.3% Justice. The Star never stands at the centre of a personal chart for any date: this card appears only in a couple.

Waite quotes the mottoes of The Star and calls them true: “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”. Wen writes of hope, inspiration and “divine charity”, a generosity that gives more than it receives. In the novel The Star is hidden in the coldest man. “Whenever he knew that money was needed for a noble, useful, or benevolent purpose, he supplied it quietly and sometimes anonymously”; his winnings at whist went to his charities. The thousand pounds left after the wager he divides between Passepartout and Fix, the detective who arrested him. Outside, mechanics; inside, a quiet spring.

In a couple, The Star at the centre is a union that inspires both: next to each other the two understand who they want to be. On the downside, in Lisovskaya, the same Star enjoys being in love and backs away from responsibility when the question of marriage or a child comes up. The atmosphere and the main task rhyme here: on the downside The Star and The Fool stumble over the same serious step, and on the upside both cards give a hope that needs no receipt.

In 3.3% of couples with this tail Justice holds the centre, and the atmosphere is different: honest accounts and clear duties. This is the Fogg who deducts from Passepartout's share “the cost of the gas which had burned in his room for nineteen hundred and twenty hours, for the sake of regularity”, while they were travelling. The values of such couples are always The Lovers.

The couple's values answer what the union is for. The Lovers (71.1%) make it a union for choosing: choosing each other again and again, as Aouda chooses Fogg with her question “will you have me?”. The Devil (28.9%) makes it a union for sorting out its bonds: which hold by choice, and which by habit, by fear, or like a wager that can no longer be lost. With this tail The Devil appears among the values only when The Star is at the centre.

The dates 08.01.1976 and 14.08.1975 give the couple's tail 21-7-22. The first partner's personal tail is 6-20-14, the second's 15-5-8; this is the rarest of the four combinations, 16% of such couples.

The middle is calculated from the two personal middles, not from the couple's outer numbers: 20 + 5 = 25, and 25 reduces to 2 + 5 = 7. The couple's centre is 10 + 7 = 17, The Star. The couple's values are 15, The Devil. And this couple has The Fool at one more point, “How you are seen”: 8 + 14 = 22. That happens in 4.3% of couples with this tail: The Fool, which is a task for the two of them, looks to others like lightness, brightness and a touch of frivolity.
The compatibility calculator on the site works out every point itself: just enter two dates of birth.

sections.h2: How the loop of this tail turns
paragraphs: The loop is recognised by repetition. First the shared world: the two sit down again and draw a plan — a new country, a new home, a new life. Then The Chariot: tickets, deadlines, arrangements, a race in which there is no time to ask “how are you”. Then a serious step comes up, and it is not on the schedule. One disappears into work, the other takes offence. Someone says “let's not spoil everything with formalities”, someone gets jealous because it is unclear what they have a right to. And the couple returns to the start — to a new plan that once again promises the whole world.

The price of the loop is years in three cabins. Side by side, with flawless care for each other, and nobody knows what is between them. Weariness from a speed nobody chose. And the feeling of always running late, although in fact there is a day in hand.

ul: **Name the status in words.** Not “it will sort itself out”, but Aouda's question: what are we to each other. It is a conversation, not an item on the plan.
**Do not wait for the edge.** In the novel the proposal comes on the day of ruin. A couple need not be brought to the brink to say the main thing — Passepartout is right: “Never too late.”
**Mention the error instead of resetting the other's watch.** Each has their own time, and almost always both are right, like Poe's captains. It is enough to notice the difference and agree on it.
**Keep a day off the timetable.** A shared calendar needs a day with nothing booked — not a planned rest, but an empty square.
**Do not burn the cabins.** Sleep, weekends, home and the talk about “us” are not firewood for speed.
**Value the detour.** The shortest route belongs to The Chariot; meetings happen on detours.
**Give freedom without checking up.** And live by the same rules one expects of the other.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 21-7-22 tail
paragraphs: On the upside this is one of the freest stories two people can have. The world for them is a living horizon, not a table: they travel a lot, move easily, can live in different countries and never lose their common language. The Chariot is their shared vehicle, not their master: they decide quickly, protect each other, and each has their own road. The Fool becomes trust: no checking up is needed, starting from zero holds no fear, and the two can laugh at what others call a disaster.

The novel's last chapter is called “In which it is shown that Phileas Fogg gained nothing by his tour around the world, unless it were happiness”. And its last lines are a question: “What had he really gained by all this trouble? What had he brought back from this long and weary journey? Nothing, say you? Perhaps so; nothing but a charming woman, who, strange as it may appear, made him the happiest of men!”
For Waite The Fool is zero. The strong version of the 21-7-22 tail is a couple that has gone round a whole world and brought home “nothing”: the main thing, which fits into no timetable.

ul: **21 · The World — “Entry to the task”.** The shared wish that brings the two of them into the task: a whole world — shared views, open space, the road. The same point is the couple's “Common language”. The resistance hides here too: a world drawn together once is no longer redrawn.

**7 · The Chariot — “Middle of the task”.** How the couple travels the road: in motion, projects and moves, with a clear route and victories over obstacles. The risk is that the union turns into a timetable, and the heart gets whatever time is left “when there is time”.

**22 · The Fool — “Main task”.** What the couple has to learn: to name what they are to each other and take the serious step not as an escape and not on schedule, but freely. On the downside: an easy start, years of uncertainty and a swerve away whenever things come to the point.

intro: This tail is lived almost word for word in a novel everyone read as a child and hardly anyone read as the story of a couple. In Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days, Phileas Fogg stakes his fortune on the whole world, crosses it by the timetable and wins only because his bride proposes to him on a day that was not on his calendar. The novel's decisive mix-up is between 21 and 22 December.

faq.q: What does the 21-7-22 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple with The World (21) at the entry to the task, The Chariot (7) in the middle and The Fool (22) as the main task. The two quickly find a shared picture of life and travel the road in motion and to a plan. What they have to learn is the serious step, clarity about what they are to each other, and a freedom that rests on trust rather than on escape.

faq.q: Is it a hard tail? Does it mean the couple will not marry?
faq.a: No. The tail predicts no weddings, break-ups or dates. It shows where the couple finds things easy — in a shared world and in motion — and where it skids: in an unnamed status and before serious steps. The strong version of this tail is a free couple that knows how both to travel and to stay.

faq.q: Why does the 21-7-22 tail never occur in a personal chart?
faq.a: In a personal chart the tail's entry M equals the main task D plus the centre, and with D = 22 an entry of 21 is impossible with any centre. In a couple each point is the sum of two personal ones, so the entry 21 is made of 15 + 6 or 12 + 9, and the tail becomes possible.

They share the middle and the main task — The Chariot and The Fool — but the entry differs. In 12-7-22 the couple enters the task through The Hanged Man, through pause and waiting; in 3-7-22 through The Empress, home and plenty; in 21-7-22 straight through a whole world. The numbers 21, 7 and 22 form no other couple tail in a different order: this order is the only one.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether they have the 21-7-22 tail?
faq.a: Enter both dates of birth in the compatibility calculator: it adds up the matching points of the two charts and shows the three numbers in the sphere “The couple's karmic tail”. For example, the dates 08.01.1976 and 14.08.1975 give exactly 21-7-22, with The Star at the centre and The Devil among the values.

faq.q: What changes if the couple's centre holds Justice instead of The Star?
faq.a: That happens in 3.3% of couples with this tail, and their values are then always The Lovers. The atmosphere rests on honest accounts and clear duties. The Fool's task is the same, but next to it the question “what are we to each other” easily shrinks to “who has put how much into the shared road”.

report: Phileas Fogg, in Jules Verne's novel, won his wager on the whole world only because his bride proposed to him on a day that was not on his calendar. The 21-7-22 tail tells the same story. The couple's task opens with The World — the last card of the Major Arcana, the end of the road — passes through The Chariot and closes with The Fool, the card of beginnings. A couple with this tail starts from a whole world, and what it has to learn is the first step.

report.h3: A world where everything is “All included”

A couple burns sleep, weekends and the home where one can simply be in the same way.

The main task is The Fool, and it is read through what does not work. Above all, that means uncertainty. Aouda, once rescued, travels with Fogg for eighty days, and her position is never named: “engage three cabins.” He looks after her flawlessly, but “with the precision of an automaton”, and she “did not quite know what to make of him”.

A couple with this tail can live for years in such a “for now”: together, but without a name. Everything begins easily and beautifully, and as soon as it comes to a serious step — moving in, getting married, moving abroad together — one of them suddenly has an urgent trip or a new project, a “let's do it later”. The freedom both were proud of becomes two flatmates with a shared calendar. The one who dislikes rules starts to be jealous and to check up, and at the first difficulty walks out with a reproach.

In the novel it is Aouda who leaps, at the worst moment. Fogg is sure he arrived five minutes late and is ruined. “I have need of nothing.” “I have no friends, madam.” “I have no longer any relatives.” Then she rises: **“Mr. Fogg, do you wish at once a kinswoman and friend? Will you have me for your wife?”** For eighty days the status had no name — and now it is named in one sentence.

report.h3: The day a serious step gave back

report: Passepartout runs to the Reverend to arrange the wedding for Monday and comes back without his hat: “Because to-morrow—is Sunday!… No—to-day is Saturday.” Travelling east, towards the sun, Fogg gained a day without knowing it. He lived the whole day as 22 December, and it was the 21st, with ten minutes left before the wager closed.

Fogg names the cause of his victory himself: **“If you had not suggested our marriage, my servant would not have gone to the Reverend Samuel Wilson's, I should not have been apprised of my error, and—”** The error was uncovered not by calculation and not by speed, but by the decision to marry. That is the hidden plot of the 21-7-22 tail: **the main task is not the price of the road but the key to it.** While the two race by the timetable, they feel they are late and have lost everything. Clarity about what they are to each other gives back time that, it turns out, was in hand all along.

What changes the loop. Name the status in words and do not wait for the edge: a couple need not be brought to the brink to say the main thing. Do not reset the other's watch; notice the difference instead. In the first chapter Fogg says of his servant's slow watch: “No matter; it's enough to mention the error.” Keep a day in the shared calendar with nothing booked. Do not burn the cabins. And value the detour: the morning after the wedding Passepartout worked out that the world could have been gone round in seventy-eight days, “by not crossing India”. But without India there would have been no Aouda.

On the upside this is one of the freest stories two people can have. The world for them is a living horizon, not a table. The Chariot is their shared vehicle, not their master: they decide quickly and protect each other, and each has their own road. The Fool becomes trust: no checking up is needed, and starting from zero holds no fear. Verne's last chapter is called “In which it is shown that Phileas Fogg gained nothing by his tour around the world, unless it were happiness”.
